"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.

Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.

The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.

Crosetto said that victory for Ukraine would be "a victory for peace, a victory for justice, a victory for international law".

He vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting Italy's parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.

The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.

At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".

Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".

But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.

Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'

Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.

During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms instead of education.

Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."

In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.

But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".

"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."

Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.

The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".

A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.

But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.

"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
ir_summary: Italian defense minister criticizes Trump's policy on limiting US support for Ukraine, warning it prolongs the war.

title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
text:
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning,we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.

The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.

"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons.  They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head.  His elderly mother was also injured.

Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.

"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.

Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.

The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.

Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack.  He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.

All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.  Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack.  So all the families are working together today."

But the tactic doesn't work today.  As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.

There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field.  Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate.  We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action.  Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat.  Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.

American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said.  "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag.  I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."

In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

Despite the video evidence and testimony, the Israeli prime minister's office said the facts remained unclear and were under investigation.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.

As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.

Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.

The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.

Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.

What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

'Taking in my great-grandkids at 74 saved me'
ir_summary: Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and a journalist during olive harvest in West Bank, injuring multiple people including US citizens.

title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
text:
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response togambling and substance addiction,external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve upcontent which harms users' mental health,external, and that they'respreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist -who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia- came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive –although a US jury recently ruled otherwise.

"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.

Right-wing parties in Australia –and the Trump administration– have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.

The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far,it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience,"researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation,external.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.

Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.

"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."

Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."

Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.

Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.

"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are availablefrom BBC Action Line.
ir_summary: Australia proposes laws forcing social media platforms to allow users to disable algorithmic content recommendations to protect mental health.

title: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
text:
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?

For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.

This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.

The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collectivewhich began as a joke- led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.

Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief,ended in a police crackdown.

Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.

Delhi Policesays,externalit acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.

Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.

Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.

In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.

Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.

Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.

Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament.

"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote ina 2023 paper,external.

Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.

Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.

Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.

It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance.

"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.

Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmarkrural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar.

"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.

Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".

But sustaining a protest for months was not easy.

Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.

In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.

A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.

When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time.

"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.

Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.

It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.

In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night.

"Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks.

While Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture.

Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance.

"We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says.

When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said.

She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar.

She sees signs of that inprotests by farmerswho camped at Delhi's borders for months, and peoplewho sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhooddemanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law.

Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi.

It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed".

As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?
ir_summary: Delhi Police ends Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, redirecting demonstrations to distant, costly venues after Supreme Court suggestion.

title: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
text:
Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.

As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races.

Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?

Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.

The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.

While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump,a Reuters analysis indicated,externalthat two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.

Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.

"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.

"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.

Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.

Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.

In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.

She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.

Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.

During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked aboutthe Trump administration striking a deal with Russiato import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.

The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."

As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.

The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.

Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.

He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".

On Thursday, a protester interrupted the Maine debate and Collins suggested the disrupter was associated with her opponent.

Jackson hit back at Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."

Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and congressman Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.

What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".

Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.

In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".

Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness".

"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.

There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.

One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico,a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.

Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win.Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.

Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton has not accepted any of those invitations.

In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign and Paxton have said little on the matter.

Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has urged the candidates to debate.

"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weeklyUS Politics Unspunnewsletter. Readers in the UK cansign up here. Those outside the UK cansign up here.

As Michigan Senate race heats up, Vance calls El-Sayed 'evil'
ir_summary: US Senate midterm debates show Republican candidates navigating loyalty to Trump amid voter concerns over economy and tight races.

title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
text:
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.

Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.

This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.

While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September –  and suffered few casualties in return.

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".

Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.

He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.

This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.

Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.

Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.

Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.

Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.

Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.

The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.

An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."

He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.

Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".

"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."

Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.

In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.

"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."

"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".

That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.

"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.

"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."

All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.

Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.

But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.

The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.

I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."
ir_summary: Ukrainian forces conduct a successful counter-offensive operation against Russia in Donbas, liberating territory and inflicting heavy casualties.

title: Govt files review plea against SC ruling to move Imran to Shifa International Hospital, terms it 'discriminatory'
text:
ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Wednesday filed a petition in the Supreme Court, seeking a review and recall of the SC order to shift incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan to Islamabad's Shifa Inte­rn­ati­onal Hospital for medical examination and treatment.

The government's review petition, filed by Islamabad Advocate General Naveed Hayat Malik on behalf of the federal capital's chief commissioner a day after theSC's ruling, termed the interim order "discriminatory".

The petition, a copy of which is available withDawn, stated that the order was "in excess of jurisdiction" and, therefore, "liable to be reviewed".

The plea further stated that the order "suffers from errors of law floating on the surface of the record".

It argued that Rule 197 of the Pakistan Prison Rules, 1978, which governs the manner and mode of the transfer of a prisoner to the hospital, had escaped SC's attention in its ruling on Imran's hospitalisation.

"Had the court taken note of the above-noted provision of law, the order under review could not have been passed," the plea said.

Elaborating on Rule 197, the plea stated that it explained that government orders for the transfer of a prisoner would be obtained through the police inspector general (IG) in cases wherein a convicted or under-trial prisoner was to be admitted to the hospital for treatment.

However, in emergency cases, the jail superintendent was authorised to act as if the government sanction had been given, and if he did so, he should immediately inform the IG, the plea added, citing the rule.

Under the rule, in cases where a prisoner was to be moved to a hospital for an operation, the shifting should take place as close as possible to the time fixed for the operation, and the prisoner should be brought back to the prison hospital "as soon as this can conveniently be done", the plea said.

Moreover, it contended that issuing directives for the treatment of a convict at a private hospital, and that too on the basis of a report that did not disclose any condition requiring immediate medical treatment, "will severely disturb the entire criminal justice system".

Here, the mention of a report was a reference to the onesubmittedto the SC by the Adiala jail superintendent on Imran's health, a day before the court's interim order.

The petition also cited Article 25 of the Constitution, highlighting that it granted the fundamental right to be treated equally and that the "Constitution abhors discrimination and favouritism".

It argued that "similarly placed convicts will claim the same special treatment afforded to the respondent (Imran) in violation of the prison rules".

The SC order, therefore, was "discriminatory in nature as similarly placed prisoners have not been afforded the same opportunity of medical treatment at a private hospital of their own choosing", the petition said.

"If the interim order is not recalled, it will open a floodgate of prisoners seeking similar relief, which under the prevalent law, cannot be granted," it added.

The plea also highlighted that the petition for Imran's hospitalisation had the Islamabad district election commissioner nominated as one of the respondents. "But no notice was issued to him before the order. Thus, the August 18 order is liable to be recalled for being in violation of the principles of natural justice," it contended.

Moreover, it highlighted that Article 10-A of the Constitution guaranteed the right to a fair trial and due process.

"Due process encompasses a fair notice of hearing to both parties. In the present case, the criminal appeal was fixed for the first time, and as such, no notice of hearing has been issued by the bench nor leave to appeal has been granted by the court," the review petition contended.

It further argued that the petition for Imran's hospitalisation "itself raised serious questions as to its maintainability", adding that this matter was also raised by the law officer in the court.

"Yet, the court postponed the serious question as to the maintainability of the petition, and on the basis of a report submitted in a connected matter, formed a prima facie opinion that the report indicated deteriorating health of the respondent, whereas nothing in the report suggested that Imran Khan's condition was any worse."

It argued that the court had even "failed to appreciate that the respondent has been medically examined regularly and treated by a medical board multiple times, adding that the SC had repeatedly held that the court should not interfere in matters that required a technical and professional skill set as the court lacked such expertise.

The plea stated that in the given circumstances, the "proper course for the court was to seek advice of the medical expert on the report and thereafter decide if it discloses any worsening of the condition of the respondent".

"There is no gainsaying that Imran Khan is a convict and has to be treated in accordance with law like any other convict," it asserted.

The plea said the jurisprudence for the grant of interim relief was well settled: "a court seized of a lis (lawsuit) can only grant relief in the interim that was intermediary, and in no case final relief can be granted at the interim stage".

It went on to list the prayers made in the plea for Imran's hospitalisation, which included him being moved to Shifa International Hospital for eye treatment; access to his personal physicians who may be associated with all the procedures of examination and treatment; family members being informed about his treatment and checkup and being provided access to him at these instances; provision of his medical report/reports of checkups to his lawyers.

The government stated in its plea that the SC had accepted all four requests in totality as an interim measure. It contended that SC had decided the lawsuit at the interim stage without any notices being issued to the respondents.

"There is nothing left to adjudicate upon. Such a course is unwarranted by the law and has always been frowned upon by the Supreme Court. Therefore, the August 18 order is in violation of the settled principle of law as expounded by the Supreme Court, and accordingly, the same is liable to be set aside," the petition argued.

The petition is yet to be fixed for hearing.

According to Order IV, Rule 28 of the Supreme Court Rules as amended in 2025, the application for a review has to be fixed before the same bench that delivered the judgement — which in this case would be a three-judge bench headed by Justice Shahid Waheed and comprising Justices Naeem Akhtar Afg­­han and Ishtiaq Ibr­ahim.

The rules state that in case the author judge — Justice Waheed in this case — recuses or resigns, the application will be heard by a bench comprising one or more judges of the bench that delivered the judgement or order sought to be reviewed.

After the final disposal of the application for review, no subsequent application for a review on the same issue can be filed to the court, and the court registry will not accept any such plea, according to the rules.

In its interim order on Tuesday, the SC directed the government to shift Imran to Shifa Inte­rn­ati­onal Hospital within two days for examination and treatment by a multidisciplinary medical board.

The court also allowed his personal physician and sister to remain associated with his medical care and directed authorities to facilitate regular family contact.

The court said the directions were being issued as an interim arrangement, without prejudice to the rights and contentions of the parties, and must be complied with by the government, its officers and agencies "in letter and spirit" until the next hearing on September 16.

It further directed the government to place before it Imran's complete medical record from the date of his arrest, including tests, reports, prescriptions, medical opinions and details of treatment administered to him.

The authorities were also asked to provide details of meetings held during the preceding three months between Imran and his family members and lawyers, as well as complete details of cases in which he was accused, arrested, facing trial or had been convicted and sentenced.

The court directed authorities to facilitate meetings between Imran and his family once a week and allow him to speak to his sons by telephone twice a week.

Until the next hearing, Imran's family members, PTI members and lawyers associated with him have been barred from disclosing his health condition or medical reports to the media or public.

The court also directed the PTI and Imran's family to ensure that no public gathering took place on the hospital premises and ordered that his medical reports or information concerning his health should not be used for political purposes.

It warned that non-compliance could lead to withdrawal of facilities granted under the order.

The government was also directed to make adequate security arrangements during Imran's stay at the hospital.

Hours after the court order, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tararsaidin a video statement that the government would ask the SC to make "suitable modifications" to its order regarding Imran Khan's health, including shifting him to a government hospital for treatment instead of a private facility.

The order was issued on a set of pleas filed by the PTI,Imran himself, and his family, seeking the former premier's transfer to Shifa Inter­national Hospital, access to personal physicians, family and counsel and the disclosure of his medical details.

It came a day after the superintendent of the Adiala jail — where Imran has been imprisoned since Aug 2023 —submitteda report to the SC on the ex-premier's health condition.

In the report, the jail administration said adequate healthcare facilities were being provided to Imran and medical officers visited him thrice a day, checking his meals and recording his blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation.

However, an annexure to the report stated that Dr Akhtar Ali Bandeshah of  the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) examined him on Aug 1 and noted complaints of uncontrolled and fluctuating blood pressure, palpitations, headache and restlessness. The ex-premier had attributed his symptoms and stress partly to infrequent meetings with his wife, family and social contacts, as well as the absence of newspapers and TV.

The doctor recommended measures to reduce mental stress, including more frequent meetings with his wife and access to reading material. He also recommended a CT coronary angiography and an increase in BP medication, noting that the 74-year-old PTI leader faced a risk of complications.

On August 10, a medical board comprising Pims specialists examined him after he complained of heaviness in the head and palpitations, the SC was informed. It recommended a one-hour daily walk and relaxation in his prison routine, besides access to newspapers, magazines, television and books.

The board also recommended more frequent interaction with immediate family members or his spouse, saying this could help control his anxiety and blood pressure.

Imran's health has turned out to be a sticking point between the government and the opposition PTI in recent months, with Imran having been taken to Pims for treatment multiple times after hiseye ailment— right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) —came to lightin late January.

The PTI and the government have been engaged in ablame game, with the latteraccusingthe former of a lack of transparency in not ensuring appropriate treatment for Imran.
ir_summary: Pakistan's government challenges Supreme Court order to move Imran Khan to hospital, calling it discriminatory.

title: Pakistan condemns ‘unprovoked’ Israeli attack on Syria air base
text:
The Foreign Office (FO) on Wednesday strongly condemned the "unprovoked" attack carried out by Israel on an air base in Syria, saying such acts had the potential to "further undermine regional peace and stability".

Syria's state-runEkhbariyatelevision, citing a military source,saidon Tuesday that Israel carried out eight airstrikes on the runway and storage facilities at the Abu al-Duhur base near Aleppo in northwest Syria. A separate military source and a civilian who lived near the base said there were no casualties.

"Such provocative actions constitute a flagrant violation of international law and have the potential to further undermine regional peace and stability," the FO said on Wednesday.

"Pakistan expresses its unwavering solidarity with the brotherly people of Syria, and reiterates its full support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity as well as peace and prosperity of the Syrian Arab Republic," the FO said.

Pakistan also called on the international community to play its role in ending repeated violations of international law by Israeli occupation forces and to hold them accountable for their destabilising actions in the region, it added.

US envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said on Tuesday it was confirmed that Israel carried out the strikes on the air base in Idlib province.

The attacks "constitute an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability", Barrack, a business friend of President Donald Trump who is also ambassador to Turkey, wrote on X.

"We encourage all parties to prioritise logical discourse over further military incidents," he said.

The strike marked extraordinary defiance by Israel of the United States, which has sought to support Syria's new government allied with Turkiye.

"Israel and Syria agreed to a status quo in security matters, which Syria was on the verge of breaching by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at an airbase near Aleppo," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said in a statement after a day of official silence by Israel.

"Israel repeatedly warned Syria that such a deployment would pose a threat to Israel's security. Syria chose to ignore these warnings," said the statement, which stopped short of acknowledging Israeli responsibility.

Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shibani called for the attacks to stop, saying Israel should recalculate its position toward Syria because it was confronting not only Damascus, but also Syria's allies.

"These attacks don't have security justifications … We will continue in our diplomatic path to dissuade Israel from this policy and to force it to stop its attacks on Syria," he said at a press conference with International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi in Damascus.

Meanwhile, the Turkish government slammed Israel's remarks in a statement on Wednesday quoted by theAnadolustate news agency.

"The frivolous allegations put forward by the Israeli Prime Minister's office aim to legitimise Israel's unlawful airstrikes targeting Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity," it said.

The base, about 70 km (43.5 miles) east of the Turkish border, has been out of service as a dedicated military airfield since 2013 and changed hands several times during Syria's 14-year civil war between forces loyal to former president Bashar al-Assad and opposition factions.

Israel has repeatedly struck Syrian forces sinceAssad was ousted in 2024. It has so far attacked mostly government sites in southern and central Syria, most recently in March.
ir_summary: Pakistan condemns Israeli airstrikes on Syrian air base as violation of international law.

title: PM directs petroleum minister to travel to Karachi, hold talks with oil refineries for reducing diesel prices
text:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday directed Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik to travel to Karachi and hold negotiations with oil refineries to reduce diesel prices, the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) said.

The premier issued the directive during a meeting with the petroleum minister, which Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Khan Cheema, Climate Change Minister Dr Musadik Malik, and MNA Hamza Shehbaz also attended.

According to the PMO, the prime minister directed Malik to "immediately" reach Karachi and take steps for providing the public relief with regard to fuel prices.

It said he directed the minister to "hold negotiations with the oil refineries" and "ensure measures to reduce the price of locally produced diesel".

"The petroleum minister himself should complete negotiations with the refineries as soon as possible to reduce its prices. As much relief as possible should be provided to the public immediately," it said.

The development comes after the government on Tuesdayraisedthe price of petrol by Rs3.34 per litre and that of high-speed diesel by Rs5.27 under its daily pricing mechanism, which wasintroducedamid global oil disruptions due to the Middle East conflict.

Last week, the Pakistan Petroleum Dealers' Association (PPDA) had given the federal government a72-hour ultimatum, accusing it of failing to honour assurances made by the petroleum minister regarding its demands.

The dealers had sought replacement of the existing fixed margin with a variable margin linked to the retail prices of petrol and diesel, proposing that it be set at 8pc of the retail price of both fuels.

In a move aimed at averting the nationwide strike, the government on Fridayapproveda 15.5 per cent increase in dealers' margins on both petrol and high-speed diesel.

The decision raised the dealers' margin on both fuels by Rs1.34 per litre, from Rs8.64 to Rs9.98 per litre. The revised margin is scheduled to take effect from Sept 1.

The shift from fortnightly to daily petroleum price revisions added another demand from dealers, who sought to link their margins to retail prices. The government, however, decided toretainthe daily pricing mechanism.
ir_summary: Pakistani PM directs petroleum minister to negotiate with oil refineries to reduce diesel prices for public relief.

title: Israel opens criminal probes over killings of Hind Rajab and Gaza rescue workers, military says
text:
Israel's military will open internal criminal investigations over its troops' killings in Gaza of Hind Rajab in January 2024 and 15 emergency and aid workers in March 2025, it said on Wednesday.

The military said the investigation decisions followed probes by its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism. It released decisions regarding five incidents involving the deaths of Palestinians.

They included an examination of the killings of seven aid workers with the World Central Kitchen charity in April 2024. On that incident, the military claimed there was "no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation."

"For more than a thousand days, the IDF (Israel Defence Forces) has been conducting intensive combat across numerous fronts, carrying out a wide range of military missions in an exceptionally complex operational reality," the Israeli military said.

"As part of the IDF's obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law, the IDF examines exceptional incidents that occurred during combat," the military said.

In January 2024, six-year-old Hindpleadedto be rescued, after her family's car came under fire in war-ravaged Gaza City, leaving her alone, frightened and injured, surrounded by the bodies of her dead relatives.

"I am so scared," she had said in a desperate phone call to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS).

After more than two weeks of frantic efforts to reach her, Hind's body, along with those of her relatives and two PRCS workers who had been dispatched to rescue her, was recovered.

An independent investigation by the London-based research group Forensic Architectureanalysedsatellite imagery and visual evidence, concluding that several Israeli tanks were near the vehicle and that one fired 335 rounds at the car carrying Hind and her family. The group also suggested that a tank likely attacked the ambulance.

Hind's story and the recording of her emergency call later became the basis for the docudrama "The Voice of Hind Rajab" by Tunisian filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania.

The film wasnominatedfor best international feature film in the Academy Awards this year. The film incorporates real audio from Hind's call to Red Crescent emergency workers.

In March this year, US lawmakersintroducedlegislation demanding a US investigation into Hind's killing.
ir_summary: Israel's military opens criminal investigations into killings of Palestinian civilians and aid workers in Gaza.

title: Govt launches mobile app for small traders’ tax scheme
text:
The government on Wednesday launched a mobile application for its Fixed Tax Asaan Scheme, allowing small traders and shopkeepers to file their tax returns through the app.

The government hadunveiledthe scheme ahead of presenting the federal budget for traders with an annual turnover of up to Rs200 million.

Addressing a press conference alongside Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb and representatives of the trader community, Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani said the launch marked the "practical start" of a project the government had been working on for the past few months.

Kayani congratulated the trader community on the successful launch of the app, saying it had been developed with their "guidance and consultation".

He recalled that the tax scheme for small traders was announced ahead of the budget on June 5. Following the announcement, the government team worked on developing the app and the plates to be provided to shopkeepers.

The minister said the government team kept trader representatives Ajmal Baloch and Kashif Chaudhry, along with their associates, in the loop throughout the app's development.

"We initiated the process with a few questions: why had tax schemes in the past failed, and what was required to make a scheme successful today — one that would make it easier for traders to become tax filers while helping achieve the twin objectives of expanding the tax net and increasing the number of tax filers?" Kayani said.

He said the scheme had been designed as a "win-win for all", with the government benefiting from increased tax collection while traders would have a simpler, more facilitative system and easier dealings with the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR).

"This is a trader-led scheme and it will be successful with trader-led implementation," he noted.

The minister outlined the key features of the scheme and app, saying it was open to all traders, whether they were already tax filers or not, provided their annual sales did not exceed Rs200 million.

Kayani said the app contained a simple form in Urdu and could be downloaded from the Google Play Store, where an "Asaan Tajir" icon had been added.

A PSID will be generated during the registration process, allowing traders to pay their tax through the app, he said. Once the payment is made, users will be notified of their inclusion in the scheme and their updated tax-filer status. They will also be informed about the benefits available to them under the scheme.

Traders who avail themselves of the facility will receive a digital version of the plate. "No FBR official can enter the premises of a shop displaying the plate to question the trader on tax matters," Kayani said.

Kayani added that a physical copy of the plate would be available from the relevant office within two weeks.

Clarifying the tax calculation, Kayani said the amount payable would be one per cent of declared sales, with withholding tax deducted from the amount. Traders would have to pay a minimum of Rs25,000 in tax, while the app would calculate the amount payable for each trader.

Existing tax filers can also benefit from the scheme, provided their sales did not exceed Rs200 million in each of the last three years. However, their minimum tax liability would be equal to the amount they paid in the previous year.

The minister also said traders who opted for the scheme would not be required to install point-of-sale (POS) machines at their shops or act as withholding agents.

He added that the app would be available on the Apple Store in the coming days.

"Currently, the app is available in Urdu. However, as promised, it will be made available in other languages, including Pashto, Balochi and Sindhi, by the first week of September," he said.

Kayani said traders would also be provided assistance, if required, in approaching the relevant focal offices and focal persons at the Regional Tax Offices (RTOs) in each district.

He said the government would continue implementing the scheme in consultation and partnership with traders. The government would also guide and assist chambers of commerce, which, he added, had an important role to play in the process.

The state minister displayed the physical plate, saying it had all the required security features. He added that traders who registered under the scheme by the tax-filing deadline would receive the plate free of cost. The plate was expected to cost no more than Rs1,500, he said.

Addressing the press conference, Aurangzeb said traders, particularly small businessmen, expected the government to provide them with an easy and simple tax scheme.

He expressed hope that the government's efforts would succeed, saying the entire process of developing the scheme and app had been carried out in consultation with traders.

The finance minister said he and Kayani had discussed the matter in parliament, the Senate and the National Assembly's finance committees, stressing the importance of consultation.

He added that the FBR had "gone out of its way" to make the scheme convenient for small traders. "He (the trader) would believe that it will work this time and that he will not face harassment or other issues if he comes under the tax net," he said.

Aurangzeb also thanked the two leaders of the trader community present at the press conference for helping take the initiative forward with the same objective.

"The tax system doesn't work if any strata of Pakistan is not covered under the mainstream," he said, adding that people had to deal with the FBR, the country's tax authority.

He noted that it was the government's responsibility to make the tax-filing system easy for people and free from harassment.

The minister said previous schemes had been "one-size-fits-all". However, "this time a few changes have been made, including a distinction between small shopkeepers and enterprises that operate on the retail side".

Traders could either opt for the regular scheme or join the newly launched scheme, the finance czar added, urging all traders not to miss the opportunity.
ir_summary: Pakistan's government launches a mobile app for small traders to file taxes under the Fixed Tax Asaan Scheme.

title: Digital platforms need to take Pakistan's 'specific circumstances' into account, minister tells Google delegation
text:
Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry on Wednesday told a delegation from Google that digital platforms would have to take the country's "specific circumstances" into account.

According to the interior ministry, Chaudhry met a delegation from the tech giant led by Senior Director David Weller. Google Pakistan's representative Kyle Gardner was also part of the delegation.

It said the meeting covered digital security, the effective use of social media against terrorism, the timely regulation of online content and mutual cooperation.

"Pakistan wishes to further enhance cooperation and coordination with Google for a safe and peaceful digital environment," Chaudhry was quoted as saying.

He said that Pakistan's geographical location was "different from other countries".

"Digital platforms will have to take into account the specific circumstances of Pakistan," he said, adding that terrorists used social media to spread fear and promote terrorism.

"Given the circumstances in Pakistan, proactive monitoring of social media is essential," he said.

Meanwhile, Weller assured the minister that the company would cooperate with Islamabad to create a safe digital environment.

National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency Director General Khurram Ali, Ministry of Interior Joint Secretary Malik Sanaullah and members of the Social Media Protection and Regulation Authority were also present.

The meeting comes a day after the US-based technology giantinauguratedits local office in Pakistan at a ceremony held at the Prime Minister's House.

Speaking on the occasion, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said there was "great scope" for a fruitful partnership with Google and for strengthening bilateral ties in various areas.

Google's Global Affairs Vice President Wilson L. White had described his visit as a "big milestone".

"Google has been investing in and committed to Pakistan for over a decade, and today we have reached a milestone where we are opening a local office in Pakistan," White said.

Meanwhile, Information Technology Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja said the opening of Google's office in Pakistan would strengthen the country's talent pipeline and provide further support to the local technology ecosystem.

Talking to media, she said the presence of Google and other major international technology companies in Pakistan would encourage more global firms to establish operations in the country.

She added that Pakistan's IT exports had grown consistently by around 20 per cent over the past two and a half years, reflecting growth in the private sector. The country's freelancing economy had also exceeded $1 billion this year, she said.

Khawaja also highlighted the government's "whole-of-government" approach and the role of the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC).

She said the efforts of the SIFC, the Ministry of IT and Telecommunication and its departments had contributed to the establishment of Google's office in Pakistan.

"This is a collective collaboration and teamwork that made it possible for Google's office to open in Pakistan today," she said.
ir_summary: Pakistan's interior minister tells Google to consider the country's specific circumstances for digital security and counter-terrorism cooperation.

title: 3 'SRA terrorists' arrested for firing at Independence Day stall in Karachi, killing owner: CTD
text:
The Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) said on Wednesday that its personnel, along with those of a federal intelligence agency, had arrested three men affiliated with the banned Sindhudesh Revolutionary Army (SRA) for their involvement in firing at an Independence Day stall in Karachi.

In a statement, CTD said the stall owner was killed in the incident that took place on August 12.

"A stall selling national flags and badges was fired at in Defence Housing Authority Phase 2 near Sunset Boulevard at around 11:30pm," the statement said, adding that the stall owner was seriously wounded in the incident and later succumbed to his injuries.

The deceased — identified as Aman, a resident of Korangi's Christian Town — had set up the stall at the location since the beginning of August, CTD said.

Following the firing incident, a case was registered at the Defence police station, and CTD, along with a federal intelligence agency, launched a joint operation to apprehend the perpetrators.

"The investigation teams took the investigation forward on technical grounds and with the help of other available evidence," the press statement said.

On August 18, three terrorists were arrested in a joint operation near Korangi Causeway in Karachi, it added.

According to CTD, three hand grenades and a pistol were recovered from the arrested men, who were identified as Zafar Ali, Faraz and Sajjad Ahmad. Action was being taken against them under Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997 and Sections 4/5 of the Explosive Substances Act 1908, it said.

The statement added that the arrested men revealed during interrogation that they were affiliated with the proscribed SRA and had been tasked with targeting Independence Day stalls in Karachi. They said they received directions from an SRA member residing outside Pakistan, identifying him as Arsalan Shah.

CTD said Shah "worked to spread terrorism in Sindh at the behest of an Indian proxy".

The statement said it was found during the investigation that Sajjad had begun reconnaissance of Independence Day stalls from August 3 and decided to target the stall located in DHA Phase 2 on August 11.

On the night of August 12, Sajjad reached the site on a motorcycle, while two of his accomplices, Zafar and Faraz, were on a different motorcycle to provide him cover. Sajjad opened fire at the person present at the stall and fled the scene immediately after, the statement said.

After their arrest, they revealed that they were getting financial support from abroad "to create fear and panic in Karachi ahead of August 14".

CTD said further investigation regarding their "alleged facilitators" was under way.

"The arrested terrorists are being interrogated while a probe is also under way to trace any of their possible facilitators, coordinators outside Pakistan, sources providing them financial assistance and weapons and ammunition," the statement said, adding an investigation was also being conducted regarding their possible involvement in other incidents of crime.

The interior ministry hadbannedthe SRA in 2020, along with Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz-Aresar Group (JSQM-A) and Sindhu Desh Liberation Army (SLA) under theAnti-Terrorism Act.

SRA operatives have been found involved in multiple incidents of terrorism, and it was around this same time last year that Hyderabad CTD hadsaidit had arrested  three "most-wanted terrorists" SRA in Jamshoro during an intelligence-based operation.

"The terrorists of the banned SRA were wanted in the cases related to firing on cargo trawlers going to Punjab, especially in the areas of district Sujawal," CTD said at the time, adding that they had confessed to carrying out multiple attacks, including planting bombs on railway tracks and targeting law enforcement personnel.

In February 2024, Karachi police hadregistereda case against unidentified individuals who were said to be SRA operatives for their alleged involvement in an improvised explosive device (IED)blastnear the provincial office of the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) in Saddar. No casualties were reported in the incident.

CTD had alsoarresteda suspect said to be linked with SRA in Karachi in November 2022 for allegedly planning an attack on a Chinese doctor in Hyderabad. CTD said the funding for the planned attack was provided by SRA's Germany-based leader, Zulfiqar Khaskheli.

The banned outfit had also claimed responsibility for anIED blastin Karachi's Saddar in May 2022 that claimed the life of a man and left several others injured.
ir_summary: CTD arrests three SRA terrorists for killing a stall owner during Independence Day celebrations in Karachi.

title: Turkiye's Fidan invites Dar to attend meeting in Istanbul with Saudi, Egypt foreign ministers
text:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Wednesday invited Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar to attend the upcoming Regional 4 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Istanbul later this month.

According to the Foreign Office (FO), the development came as Dar spoke with Fidan by telephone, during which they "exchanged views on recent regional developments and discussed efforts to promote regional peace and stability".

"Fidan invited Dar to attend the upcoming Regional 4 foreign ministers' meeting of Pakistan, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, to be held in Istanbul later this month," it said.

Dar accepted the invitation and confirmed his participation in the meeting, it added. The exact date of the meeting was not immediately clear.

The two had also spoken last week andexchangedviews on the evolving regional situation and welcomed the encouraging progress towards an understanding between the United States and Iran.

Fidan had expressed hope that "these positive developments would pave the way for lasting peace and stability in the region".

The meeting in Istanbul comes as negotiations between the United States and Iran have stalled as the nearly six-month-old war grinds on with little sign of resolution.

The foreign ministers of the four countries had held two meetings ahead of the announcement of the Aprilceasefirebetween the two sides.

Thefirst meetingwas held in Riyadh on the sidelines of a consultative ministerial meeting, while thesecond meetingwas held in Islamabad. Both meetings were held in March.

The ministers of all four countries had last met in June, with the countries welcoming the signing of theIslamabad Memorandum of Understandingbetween the US and Iran.
ir_summary: Turkish FM invites Pakistan's FM to attend regional meeting with Saudi and Egyptian counterparts in Istanbul to discuss peace efforts.

title: Pakistan extends airspace ban on Indian aircraft until Sept 24
text:
Pakistan has extended its airspace ban on Indian aircraft for until Sep 24, according to a Notice to Airmen (Notam) issued by the Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA).

The extension comes as the previousrestrictionwas due to expire on Aug 23.

"Pakistan airspace not available for Indian-registered aircraft and aircraft operated or leased by Indian airlines/operators, including military flights," theNotam, issued early on Wednesday, said.

According to the Notam, the extension took effect on Aug 23 at 10:15am and will remain in force until 4:59am on Sept 24.
