Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the action as part of Operation Ghazab lil Haq, which waslaunchedon the night of Feb 26 in response to unprovokedcross-border firingby the Afghan Taliban.

Days later, Pakistanshot down eight droneslaunched from across the border that had entered Pakistani airspace near the Torkham border and Kohat. It was alsoreportedthat the Afghan Taliban engaged in unprovoked firing the night before near Kurram as security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to cross into Pakistan.

In retaliation for the drone incursion, Pakistanconducted"precision aerial and drone strikes" in 10 locations across Afghanistan.

A demarche was also delivered to the Afghan side on Sept 26 on account of the Sept 23 airspace violation by drones, the Foreign Office said.

On Oct 1, Pakistan again carried out "well-planned and calibrated"airstrikesagainst terrorist hideouts in Afghanistan, the information ministry said, which resulted in the deaths of "multiple terrorists".
ir_summary: Pakistani security forces retaliated against Afghan Taliban firing along the Kurram border, destroying posts amid ongoing border tensions.

title: Indian airlines barred from using Pakistani airspace until Nov 24 as ban extended
text:
Pakistan has extended its airspace ban for Indian aircraft for another month, until Nov 24, according to a Notice to Airmen (Notam) issued by the Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA).

Theprevious extensionof the ban was set to expire on Oct 24.

"Pakistan airspace not available for Indian registered aircraft and aircraft operated/owned or leased by Indian airlines/operators, including military flights," theNotamsaid.

According to the notice, the extension came into effect at 7:45pm on Saturday and will remain until 04:59am on Nov 24, 2026.

The country's airspace is divided into two flight information regions (FIRs) — Karachi and Lahore, according to a Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority (PCAA)documentfrom 2022.

Saturday's Notam applies to both the Karachi (OPKR) and Lahore (OPLR) FIRs.

India and Pakistanclosed their airspacesto each other's airlines in late April 2025, when tensions between themescalatedin the wake of adeadly attackin India-occupied Kashmir's Pahalgam.

On April 24, Pakistan's top brass had announced aseries of measures, including the closure of its airspace to all India-owned or Indian-operated airlines with immediate effect, as it retaliated against New Delhi's slew ofaggressive measuresagainst the country.

New Delhi, without evidence, had alleged that Islamabad backed the Pahalgam attack. However, Pakistan hadstrongly deniedany involvement and offered aneutral probe. The nuclear powers had the fiercestair battlein May, in which Pakistan said itdownedsevenIndian fighter jets.

Since then, Pakistan has extended the airspace ban several times, forcing Indian carriersto uselonger and costlier routes.

For Air India, the country's only carrier with a major international network, fuel costs rose byas much as 29 per centand journey times by up to three hours on some long-haul routes, according to a document submitted to Indian officials last October.

The airline, owned by Tata Group and Singapore Airlines, estimated the Pakistan airspace closure's impact on its profit before tax at $455 million annually — a significant amount given its fiscal 2024-25 loss stood at $439m.
ir_summary: Pakistan extends airspace ban on Indian aircraft for another month amid ongoing bilateral tensions.

title: Looting, blazes and clashes in France amid nationwide protests
text:
Police and protesters clashed violently in Paris and other French cities on Saturday on the sidelines of nationwide marches against soaring inflation, with one demonstrator's hand blown off, multiple blazes set, and looters breaking into dozens of stores to strip them bare.

With just months to go before the two-round elections in April and May to choose Macron's successor, the demonstrations follow weeks of high-schoolstudent blockadesdemanding better learning conditions.

Macron and his government were criticised by many of the demonstrators, who numbered 500,000 across the country, according to the CGT union. Authorities did not immediately give their estimate of the numbers.

Police used tear gas and water cannon against masked protesters in Paris and other cities who were throwing projectiles and aiming fireworks. Several parked cars were torched in the capital, and more than 130 arrests were made.

In the southern city of Saint-Etienne, a male protester had his hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, a police source toldAFP. His maiming came after a 15-year-old lost his hand on October 5 to a police stun grenade during another protest in the city of Lens.

The protests geared up with a handful of gatherings nationwide on Saturday morning,AFPreporters said.

In Lyon, protesters set ablaze a tourist office in the city centre, and smashed their way into town halls in the cities of Marseille and Lille, where they vandalised the premises before leaving.

Dozens of shops were looted, including many in Marseille, among them a Hermes boutique, an Apple store in Lille, several shops in Nice and at least one mobile phone outlet in Paris,AFPjournalists saw.

A crowd of more than 300 protesters tried to move up Paris's Champs-Elysees, home to flagship luxury stores. As police firing tear gas blocked their way, they yelled, "All cops are bastards".

In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.

Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.

"We've reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children," he toldAFP.

The looting and confrontations with police were being carried out by masked youths on the sidelines of marches that were largely peaceful and which attracted people of all ages, including families with children.

Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire stressed that "the overwhelming majority of demonstrators" wanted to "march calmly", but "acts of vandalism" were tarnishing their protest.

In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign".

One demonstrator, Jules Petrichor, 47, who had brought his son, said: "There was a good atmosphere and then suddenly they (the police) started gassing us, even though nothing was happening. Naturally that worsened things and the hot-heads got hot-headed."

Another protester who gave his first name as Louis, 19, complained that police were trigger-happy any time there was a demonstration.

"We can't protest any more, it's frightening," he said.

The country's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, has called Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations. It has appealed to teachers and students, workers, pensioners and farmers to take part in the protests on the first day of half-term holidays.

The principal grievance was the cost of living — pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East — that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.But there were other issues too.

High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons — the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years".

"For years we've had climate, economy and equality problems but the government is not doing anything about it," said Agnes, a 50-year-old actor who did not give her second name.

Anae, a 24-year-old student who did not give her surname, said she was protesting because she did not have a "sustainable future".

"Our planet's burning. And we've got a government that doesn't give a toss," she said.

Opposition politicians vying to succeed Macron have seized upon the protests.

Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who has sided with the police, said on X: "Looting, pillaging, attacking police — rioters have once again sullied the October 17 demonstrations over the cost of living." She claimed that the protesters' demands had been "hijacked by the far left".

Her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon, insisted early Saturday that "everything is passing off peacefully", while accusing television news of "flooding us with images of violence in dozens of cities".

Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.

"It's the Revolution — we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry of the mayor's offices.

In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death." And in the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" was unfurled above a central square.

"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.
ir_summary: Violent protests and looting in France over inflation and government policies, with police clashes and arrests.

title: Centre was compelled to impose emergency in KP, PM reiterates
text:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday reiterated that the Centre was "compelled" to impose emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa due to the provincial government's lack of cooperation in countering terrorism.

The Centreimposedemergency and governor's rule in KP on Oct 11,citingthe provincial government's "deliberate disengagement" from the fight against terrorism. The decisions were also endorsed by theParliamentthis week amid protests by the opposition.

On Saturday, PM Shehbaz visited the residence of Rashid Bashir Virk in Gujranwala to offer condolences on the demise of his father, lateMNA Mahmood Bashir Virk.

After recalling the late PML-N lawmaker's services, the premier stressed that the Centre was compelled to impose emergency in KP.

He said the Centre made a "last attempt", referring to the rounds of talks held by a joint delegation of the PPP and the government with the opposition.

The hours-long second round, held onOct 3, had endedwithout a breakthrough.

"They had talks with them (PTI) day and night, for 48 hours, and sat with the intention to settle matters from every aspect," PM Shehbaz said, adding that a draft was ready under which the PTI was to call off its long march.

The prime minister highlighted that he had held multiplemeetingswith Sohail Afridi, the KP chief minister whose role now stands non-functional, as well as with his predecessorAli Amin Gandapur.

"In every meeting, I tried my best to convey to him from the depths of my heart and with seriousness that KP is an extremely beautiful province and has very brave and honourable people, […] and I am always present in every way for their development and prosperity," PM Shehbaz said.

The premier added that he assured the KP government of the Centre's support in fighting against terrorism together to face the security challenges in the province.

PM Shehbaz said he had assured the chief minister that he would make the decisions regarding the administration, resources and necessities in consultation with him.

"But, unfortunately, despite all these efforts, thousands of our law enforcement agencies personnel, soldiers, officers and officers of the armed forces were sacrificing their lives every day to defend the homeland."

The prime minister stressed that the federal government "made many efforts" regarding the situation, but there were "threats and long marches every other day in response".

"Their past history is very horrific," he remarked, recalling the2014 sit-insstaged by the PTI at Islamabad's D-Chowk during the tenure of his brother, Nawaz Sharif.

"Last year as well, you saw how the entire country was jammed by staging a sit-in in Islamabad," he added, ostensibly referring to the PTI'sNovember 2024 protestthat had resulted in clashes.

"This time as well, they had an entire plan of bloodshed," he alleged.

The Oct 11 imposition of emergency and governor's rule followedweeksof politicaltensionsbetween the Centre and the PTI — as well asnegotiationsto bridge their differences — after the latterannounceda long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Federal ministersallegedthat the PTI-led government in KP had a "nexus" with terrorist groups and asserted that the province's security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the mainreasonsbehind thebreakdownof theirOctober 3 talks.

The PTI said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centredenied. It also called for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the lattercriticisedthe KP government's efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objected to itsstanceon dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.
ir_summary: Pakistani PM defends imposition of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa due to provincial government's lack of cooperation in counter-terrorism efforts.

title: Iran backs 'political process' to resolve Saudi-Houthi conflict
text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that Tehran supports a "political process" to resolve the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in amajor attacklast week.

"We support an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue," Araghchi said in a speech at the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad.

Araghchi repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides. Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture.

On Friday, Iran denied having anything to do with the Houthi attacks, after Saudi ArabiaaccusedTehran of encouraging the group's escalation.

In his speech, Araghchi also said "either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together," adding that Tehran was willing "to cooperate with all its brothers and neighbours to achieve the first option".

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen's coalition governmentunravelledin July.

On Wednesday, Yemen's Houthi rebels said they hadtargetedfacilities belonging to Saudi Aramco, after Saudi officials reported a strike on a building in Riyadh housing the energy giant's operations centre.

Powerful explosions also rattled the Saudi capital, as the coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a missile fired by the group towards Riyadh.

On Tuesday, Saudi Arabialaunchedstrikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, targeting fuel and energy facilities it said were being used to support missile and drone attacks, as the Yemeni group threatened a "harsh and painful" response against Saudi airports, refineries and oil installations.

Hours later, Saudi authorities issued warnings of potential hostile aerial threats in the kingdom's eastern province and Riyadh.

Loud explosions were heard near Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, according to witnesses. Later, a Saudi energy ministry official confirmed the attack. Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency said that four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital and that 15 homes were damaged.
ir_summary: Iran supports political talks to resolve the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels, offering mediation.

title: India's 'cockroach' movement founder released from police custody
text:
India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke was released from detention on Saturday, a day after he wasdetainedduring a police crackdown onprotestsagainst the election authority.

Dipke, 31, was detained on Friday in New Delhi as he headed to join a rally that the CJP protest movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district. He was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace, broadcastersNDTVand ​India Todayreported.

He walked out of a police station on Saturday afternoon, waving to the media and giving a thumbs up as he was driven away, anAFPphotographer saw.

"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.

Opposition parties and CJP activists have defied asecurity crackdown, rallying to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar afteraccusingthe poll body of manipulatingvoter rollsto benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party.

More than 130 million voters were deleted ​during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.

Student activist Neha ​Bora, a prominent face of the protests, who was also detained on Friday as she ​tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters, was released earlier on Saturday as well.

"Please, spare the people of India. ‌Impeach ⁠Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured," Bora toldANInews agency after she was released.

Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, werearrestedon Oct 14 after enteringJantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have declared off-limits for demonstrations. They remain in custody.

Members of Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls.

Rights groups and critics, however, say Modi's government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents — allegations the government rejects.

A weeks-long sit-in by supporters of the movement earlier this year forced then-education minister Dharmendra Pradhan'sresignationover ​exam paper leaks.
ir_summary: Indian activist released after detention during protests accusing election commission of voter roll manipulation.

title: Islamabad ATC summons Islamabad police chief in security breach case against Imaan and Hadi
text:
ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Saturday summoned the Islamabad police chief and issued show-cause notices to two police officials over the continued failure to produce the case record in the security breach case against lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her spouse, Hadi Ali Chattha.

Thecasepertains to the alleged disruption of a security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. Imaan and her husband were accused of removing barriers from the route. The couple wasindictedin the case on Oct 7.

During Saturday's hearing, ATC Judge Abul Hasnat Muhammad Zulqarnain directed the two police officials to whom notices were issued to explain their failure to ensure the production of the record. He warned that they could face imprisonment if it was not presented before the court.

During the proceedings, the court expressed displeasure over the continued absence of the investigating officer and raised questions about the whereabouts of the case record.

A court official informed the judge that the investigating officer had travelled to Gilgit-Baltistan and had not returned.

The judge immediately summoned the superintendent (investigation) to explain the situation.

Advocate Riasat Ali Azad, representing the accused, told the court that the bail application had been filed on October 29 last year and notices had already been issued, but the proceedings could not move forward because the investigating officer failed to appear with the record.

He argued that in similar cases, another police official usually appeared with the case record when the investigating officer was unavailable. Questioning how long the court was expected to wait, Azad urged the judge to make a decision in accordance with the law.

Advocate Asif Irfan, vice chairman of the Islamabad Bar Council, observed that the court was not powerless, but had so far been unable to ensure the production of the record.

Advocate Aleem Abbasi, meanwhile, urged the judge to exercise his authority and decide the matter on merit. He added that the legal fraternity stood with the judiciary in defending its independence, but questioned how lawyers could secure justice for their own children if the judicial system failed to deliver it.

Advocate Zafar Khokhar also questioned under which law an investigating officer could take the case record away and leave court proceedings stalled.

Judge Zulqarnain, however, expressed displeasure over the tone adopted by some lawyers, deeming such conduct inappropriate and remarking that he was not influenced by vlogs or commentary and always conducted proceedings impartially.

After a short break in the proceedings, SP Khurram Ashraf and Deputy Superintendent (DSP) Naeem Yousuf appeared before the court.

The SP informed the judge that the investigating officer had travelled to Khaplu and would appear after he returned. The judge questioned the arrangement and asked when the officer would return, observing that everyone was waiting while the court had a case to decide.

When pressed for a definite timeline, DSP Yousuf said the investigating officer could take another 10 to 15 days to return.

The judge criticised the police for causing prolonged hardship to PTI workers through delays in their cases.

Expressing frustration over the situation and the alleged harassment of workers, the judge ordered the discharge of several individuals arrested in connection with the PTI's long march.

The court subsequently issued show-cause notices to the SP and DSP, warning that failure to produce the case record could lead to proceedings for their imprisonment.

Islamabad Inspector General of Police Muhammad Sohail Chaudhry was also summoned for the next hearing on November 3.

The lawyer couple has been in jail since theirarreston Jan 23 in acaseregistered against them for protesting outside the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association president. The arrestprompted criticismby rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple's right to a fair trial.

Just a day later, a sessions courtsentencedthem to 17 years on multiple charges under thePrevention of Electronic Crimes Act(Peca) in a case pertaining to controversial social media posts. The convictions werewidelycondemned bylawyersandUnited Nations (UN) experts.

On Sept 17, followingmonths of litigationbefore thecourts, the Supreme Courtsuspendedtheir sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the IHC's final verdict on their appeals against the trial court's decision.

However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand.

The fresh case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital's Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio.

Imaan and Hadi were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added.

The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties).

They were indicted in the case on Oct 7 and the ATC on Oct 10disposedof the couple's petition seeking to drop the terrorism charges.

On Oct 15, the courtdirectedlawyers and witnesses in the case to appear at Adiala jail for the next hearing after police cited difficulties in transporting the couple to court.

At yesterday's hearing, Imaan and Hadi hadobjectedto the manner in which they were presented during the hearing of the case, with the couple and their lawyers eventually walking out of the proceedings at Adiala jail.
ir_summary: Islamabad court summons police chief over failure to produce case record in security breach case against lawyer and spouse.

title: Islamabad ATC rejects police request for physical remand of ex-GB CM Khalid Khurshid
text:
ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Saturday rejected the police's request for 30-day physical remand of PTI leader and former Gilgit-Baltistan chief ministerKhalid Khurshidand sent him to jail on judicial remand in connection with a case registered over the November 26 protest.

Judge Abul Hasnat Muhammad Zulqarnain heard the case against Khurshid. During the hearing, Islamabad police produced the PTI leader before the court and sought his physical remand for 30 days.

However, the court turned down the request and directed that he be sent to judicial custody.

A case was registered against Khurshid, the president of the PTI's GB chapter, at Aabpara Police Station in connection with the party'sNovember 26 protestin 2024.

The protest saw more than 10,000 PTI protesters surge into Islamabad, defying a ban on public gatherings and a lockdown to skirmish with 20,000 security forces enlisted to turn them back.

A day of clashes between security forces and protesters in the city's Red Zone had ended in the PTI leadership's hasty retreat, with the party announcing that it was calling off its planned protest sit-in "for the time being". Subsequently, cases were registered against several PTI leaders under various sections of the Pakistan Penal Code and Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act.

Khurshid wasarrestedalong with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati and several others at the speaker's house in Peshawar, according to the PTI, shortly after the Centreimposedemergency and governor's rule in KP on Oct 11.

Sources said Khurshid had been staying at the KP chief minister's residence since 2023 to avoid arrest by GB police.

In a separate development, the court also discharged PTI workers arrested in connection with two cases linked to the party's recent long march after rejecting a request by the investigating officer for an adjournment to conduct their identification parade.

During proceedings concerning the PTI workers arrested in two cases registered at Shalimar and Secretariat police stations, the investigating officer requested an adjournment to conduct an identification parade.

However, the defence counsel opposed the request, arguing that the workers had already spent more than 40 days in custody and that the police had repeatedly sought adjournments without producing them before the court.

The lawyers maintained that the accused were innocent and had been deliberately implicated in the cases, alleging that the police arbitrarily arrested individuals and falsely portrayed them as PTI workers.

The defence counsel reiterated their earlier plea for the discharge of the accused and urged the court to implement its order passed at the previous hearing.

Accepting the defence's arguments, the court ordered the discharge of all the PTI workers from the cases.

The workers had been placed in judicial custody for the purpose of an identification parade in connection with the cases registered at Shalimar and Secretariat police stations.
ir_summary: An anti-terrorism court rejects police request for PTI leader Khalid Khurshid's physical remand in protest case.

title: Egypt's President Sisi pledges to leave office when term ends in 2030
text:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that he would not seek to remain in office when hiscurrent termexpires in 2030, describing the matter as "completely settled".

Sisi, 71, a former army general whobecame presidentin 2014, made the remarks at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, one of his flagship megaprojects.

Speaking to graduates and state officials in the sprawling new city east of Cairo, Sisi said the Egyptian constitution "would not be touched".

"The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive. This is completely settled and there will be no discussion about it," he said.

The Egyptian constitution, approved in 2014 following the 2013 military ouster of late president Mohamed Morsi, originally limited presidents to two four-year terms.

Constitutional amendments approved in a2019 referendumextended presidential terms from four to six years and included transitional provisions that allowed Sisi to run for an additional term.

Under those amendments, Sisi wasre-elected in 2023for a six-year term that is due to expire in 2030.

Critics and opposition figures have speculated about the possibility of further constitutional changes that could allow him to remain in office beyond 2030.

Before running for president, Sisi denied having political ambitions, but he resigned from his position as defence minister in 2014 and entered the race he went on to win.

On Saturday, he said the run-up to 2030 would be used to groom a new generation of leaders, with the Military Academy training hundreds of prospective officials, ministers and presidential candidates in statecraft and leadership.

During his 12 years in power, Sisi has overseen an ambitious state-led development programme centred onmegaprojectswhich critics say have relied heavily onborrowingand contributed to Egypt's mounting debt burden and economic pressures.

Sisi's presidency has also faced sustained criticism from international human rights organisations over restrictions on political opposition, civil society andfreedom of expression, allegations the government rejects, saying its policies are necessary to preserve stability and security.
ir_summary: Egypt's President Sisi pledges to step down in 2030, ruling out constitutional changes to extend his rule.

title: Any miscalculation by adversaries will invite response beyond their ‘imagination, calculation’, warns CNSC
text:
Commander National Strategic Command (CNSC) General Aamer Raza warned the country's adversaries on Saturday that "any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or the calculation of the initiator".

"To those who harbour hostile designs across our borders, our stance remains resolute and unambiguous. There is no space for conflict or war in a nuclearised environment and any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or calculation of the initiator," warned the commander of Pakistan's strategic command.

Addressing the passing-out parade of cadets of the 154th Long Course at the Pakistan Military Academy (PMA), Kakul, he reiterated that the country's armed forces stood ready to "defend every inch of the motherland" at all costs.

The warning by thestrategic command commandercomes after provocative remarks by Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. He had warned Pakistan on Thursday that any "fresh terrorist activity from across the border would invite a strike even bigger than the last time", according to Indian news agencyANI.

Gen Raza said that in the "post-truth era", the country's adversaries sought to drive a wedge between the people of Pakistan and its armed forces through "calculated disinformation and narrative warfare".

He elaborated that following the failure ofOperation Sindoor, the adversaries sought to "fracture Pakistan's social cohesion and state infrastructure" through an escalation of proxy terrorism and sub-conventional warfare.

Gen Raza further said that hostile elements continue to attempt to exploit the country's internal vulnerabilities to "cultivate proxy instruments against our national unity".

"You must understand unequivocally that this conflict is waged directly against the security of our people and the freedom secured by the supreme sacrifices of our predecessors."

The strategic command commander added that the people of Pakistan must remain acutely mindful that safeguarding the country's unity, sovereign integrity and territorial inviolability is "an absolute imperative, which we shall uphold at all costs and under every circumstance".

Addressing the newly-graduated cadets, he added that they must remain steadfast in their duty and unwavering in their resolve and "immune to malicious propaganda and narrative warfare".

Gen Raza said the recent shifts in global geopolitics, particularly amid the escalatingconflict in the Middle East, had "once again underscored Pakistan's pivotal strategic importance on the international stage".

"Our decisive role in restoring regional stability, exemplified by the landmark Islamabad Accord, demonstrates our enduring commitment to peace and diplomacy," he said, adding that theMakkah Accordwas "a sequel to the same vision of durable peace".

Expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people, he said: "Our hearts remain heavily burdened by the ongoing tragedy in Palestine, where innocent men, women and children continue to endure unspeakable hardship and systematic oppression."

He said the Pakistani nation stood "resolute and unwavering in its diplomatic, moral and political support" for the Palestinians.

"The persistent violence, targeting of non-combatants and destruction of civilian infrastructure are profound violations of international law and a grave stain on the collective conscience of humanity," Gen Raza added.

"Today, the world witnesses increasing volatility, where grey-zone warfare and hybrid threats attempt to destabilise sovereign states," he added.

A day earlier, the Foreign Office (FO)condemnedSingh's "provocative remarks" threatening aggression against Pakistan, saying such statements highlighting the neighbouring country's "hegemonistic mindset".

"Pakistan rejects and condemns the Indian defence minister's provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India's hegemonistic mindset and the risk its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia," FO spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said.

"We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a befitting response and reply to Indian aggression," he said, referring to the brief military conflict between the two countries.

He said that there should be "no ambiguity" that Pakistan remained fully prepared to safeguard its "sovereignty and territorial integrity" against any "ill-advised aggression".

Haider said Pakistan's "restraint and commitment to peace" should not be mistaken for weakness, warning that any aggression would be met with a "forceful response".

"India should draw an appropriate lesson from last year's experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region," he said.
ir_summary: Pakistan's nuclear commander warns adversaries against miscalculation, promising overwhelming response to aggression.

title: Armed men abduct 20 under-training police personnel in Mastung: officials
text:
QUETTA: Unidentified armed men kidnapped 20 police recruits undergoing training at the Kalat Police Training Centre while they were travelling in a passenger van along the Quetta-Karachi Highway in Mastung district, officials said.

A senior Balochistan government official confirmed the abduction toDawnon condition of anonymity, saying the recruits were heading home for the weekend when armed men intercepted their van.

"Yes, 20 police personnel who were going home for the weekend were taken away by armed men while they were travelling in a passenger van on the Quetta-Karachi Highway in Mastung," the official said.

He said a group of armed men riding motorcycles and carrying automatic weapons intercepted the van and took the recruits away along with the vehicle to an undisclosed location. The armed men, however, released the driver and three other passengers travelling in the van.

Police officials in Mastung also confirmed the abduction, saying the recruits belonged to the Levies Force, which has since been merged with the police.

The abducted personnel belonged to the Rakhshan division, government officials said.

Security forces have launched a search operation in the nearby mountains to trace the abducted recruits. However, no information about their whereabouts has emerged so far.

No group has claimed responsibility for the abduction.

A day earlier, Rakhshan Division Commissioner Asad Ullah Kakar wasabductedin Balochistan's Kharan district.

In a separate incident, Kharan Deputy Commissioner Munir Ahmed Soomro wasreleasedsafely on Oct 3 after nearly two weeks in captivity following negotiations between local tribal elders and the armed men who had abducted him from the Noshki-Kharan highway the previous month.

On July 21, three excise officials werekidnappedafter an attack on a checkpost in Balochistan's Chagai district.
ir_summary: Armed men abducted 20 police recruits in Mastung, Balochistan, sparking a security forces search operation.

title: Lesser citizens
text:
FOR decades, discrimination and prejudice have narrowed the space for the country's minority communities.

TheHRCP has warnedthat non-Muslim groups subjected to themisuse of the blasphemy lawsas well as forced marriages and conversions endure constant violations of basic liberties. Its new report on the freedom of religion and belief welcomes theNational Commission for Minorities Act, 2025, and laws inPunjabandBalochistanthat set 18 as the minimum age of marriage, but expresses concerns about enforcement.

The report highlights multiple aspects of exclusion — the legal limbo facing hundreds accused of blasphemy, persecution of the Ahmadi community, abductions of minority girls, and damage to places of worship. Sadly, the institutional resolve to implement legislative measures and protect the marginalised is absent.

No citizen should have to live under a cloud of fear. Reportedly, nearly 60pc of minority students face bias, including enrolment refusals, isolation, and coercion to attend classes teaching the majority faith; 44pc of Sindh's minority children are out of school. Additionally, the 5pc public sector job quota for minority communities is largely wasted as sanitation work and lower positions are reserved for them.

These ills, made worse by poverty and the police's shoddy response, reveal that discrimination is systemic and our societal health is in bad shape. Interfaith harmony will prevail when the message to end bias is conveyed from the pulpit, alongside efforts to punish zealotry.

The formation of the National Commission for Minorities has to be immediate. Inclusivity should be embedded in school syllabi, and seminaries must be monitored regularly. The report calls on KP to raise the legal age of marriage, and recommends that consensual conversions take place in court.

But injustices will be irreversible if the power elite does not pledge safety and equality for religious communities. Above all, transforming mindsets is central to harmony.
ir_summary: HRCP report details systemic discrimination against Pakistan's religious minorities including blasphemy law misuse and forced conversions.

title: Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
text:
From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a diesel deal that could help Russia fund its war, it has been adamagingweek for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington.

Frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.

Zelensky responded to Trump's barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favouring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks.

Intensifying the discord, Trumpwaivedkey US Russia-related sanctions and tariffs on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelensky to say in a social media post that Trump's action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine.

The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelensky's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow.

Despite Zelensky's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, toldNewsmaxon Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia.

Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022full-scale invasion.

"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank.

Trump's relationship with Zelensky has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vancepublicly upbraidedZelensky during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington haspaused or slowedmilitary assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv.

The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year onenergy sitesin Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts.

Experts say thatsurgein energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.

Frustrated by Zelensky, however, Trump turned to Russia toincrease fuel supplyand contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.

In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month.

Although the law called for new penalties on Russia starting next week, it also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so.

Zelensky said that Trump's latest action undercuts the Graham Act's main goal.

"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelensky posted on X.

For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelensky said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital.

Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters.

Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelensky toldNPRthat US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders that intelligence could be reduced or cut off.

Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was disrupted after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was an order originating from the White House,Reutersreported on Thursday.

The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration.

Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom argue that Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favourable to Moscow.

Zelensky's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy.

He added that Zelensky knows who he's dealing with, and Trump's threats don't have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.
ir_summary: Tensions between Trump and Zelensky threaten US military and intelligence support for Ukraine amid the war with Russia.

title: Pakistan has enough energy supplies to last through November, planning for winter spike: Aurangzeb
text:
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Saturday toldAFPthat Pakistan had so far withstood the shock fromskyrocketingenergy prices due to theUS-Israeli war on Iran, but thatattacks on infrastructurein Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook.

In an interview on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF)-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Aurangzeb said the country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

"The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan," he said.

"We've had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries."

He added that unless the government saw "an absolute dire need", it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments.

Since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran's retaliatory action has targeted Washington's Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies.

WithYemen's civil warflaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attackedSaudi infrastructure, including energy facilities and airports, in recent days.

Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy.

"What is now [the] worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit," he said.

"I, to be very honest, I don't know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer."

Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the IMF, the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default.

It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund — at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts — since gaining independence in 1947.

With global debt stocks running high, the IMF has called at this year's annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis.

"Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while," Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile.

The country's tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts.

Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, Aurangzeb said, adding that there remained "room for improvement" on increasing income tax collection as well.

He said the government's reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests.

"Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback," he said.

The minister is leading Pakistan's delegation and is holding high-level engagements with international financial institutions, finance ministers, policymakers and investors.

Yesterday, hemetWorld Bank Group President Ajay Banga at a dinner hosted by the Thai prime minister on the sidelines of the annual meetings, state-runPakistan TVreported.

"The occasion provided an opportunity for informal interaction alongside the high-level engagements at the annual meetings", it said.

Pakistan remains engaged with the IMF under a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).

The two reached astaff-level agreementafter a fourth review under the EFF and a third review under the RSF earlier this month, which qualified Pakistan to draw about $1.2bn from the Fund's resources.
ir_summary: Pakistan's finance minister discusses energy security amid Middle East conflict and plans for winter supply needs.

title: Trump waives new Russia sanctions as Ukraine ties slump
text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, marking a new low in Washington's ties with war-torn Ukraine.

The move came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky urged EU leaders to keep financingKyiv's fightwith nearly $80 billion more next year, insisting he was standing up for his country as Trump's support slumped.

TheLindsey Graham Act— named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — had allowed Trump the authority to impose duties up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

The legislation, which Trump signed into law last month, targeted Russia's energy and defence sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.

Trump's reversal on the Russia sanctions comes after he struck a deal with Putin to ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasinglarge amounts of dieselinto global markets.

The US president'swar in Iranhas sparked crippling oil shortages and price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead ofmidterm electionsnext month.

Asked if he was being made a scapegoat for Trump's domestic woes ahead of the vote,Zelensky just smiled.

"This is my answer," he told journalists in Brussels, after an extended pause.

In another sign of strained relations between the United States and Ukraine, Trump branded Kyiv's actions a "disgrace" after Zelensky ordered his forces to resume strikes on Russian refineries.

"I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively," Zelensky said after talks with EU leaders.

Thebreakdownbetween Trump and Zelensky has fuelled fears that the US leader is siding with Moscow.

Those concerns have been heightened by disruptions to a criticalUS-provided satellite systemthat has hampered Ukraine's ability to counter Russia's intense bombardments.

Ukraine uses technology from Elon Musk's SpaceX for battlefield communications, but the tech billionaire — avirulent Zelensky critic— said his company was not behind the disruption, while a US official denied any intervention by Trump.

European leaders put on a show of unity with Zelensky as he grappled with Trump.

"This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions," European Council chief Antonio Costa said.

"Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that "the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US."

"It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today — and explore what additional steps we can take," he said.

Zelensky asked the bloc — Ukraine's biggest international backer — to provide more Patriot missiles to shoot down Russian missiles and come up with an extra 70 billion euros ($79 billion) in support next year to help Kyiv keep fighting.

Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defences ahead of winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20°C and Moscow's attacks threaten electricity, heating and water systems.

Russian strikes on the southern cities of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man and at least 17 people, including an 11-year-old girl, Ukrainian authorities said Saturday.

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that Zelensky's 70-billion euro plea "has to be covered" and urged partner countries to "step in" and help.

French President Emmanuel Macron said Kyiv's backers will analyse the demand, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the European Union will discuss it before the end of the year.

The EU is currently paying out instalments of a 90-billion-euro loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027.

But Ukrainian authorities have warned they will still face a major budget black hole as Russian strikes have battered the country's economy.

The talks on new funding have reignited calls for the EU to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.

"The frozen assets are there. That's what should be used for supporting Ukraine," said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs.

But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.
ir_summary: Trump waives US sanctions on Russian energy, worsening US-Ukraine relations amid war.

title: Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers
text:
Anthropic, the creator of the AI assistant Claude, confirmed on Friday it is circulating a draft bill among US lawmakers aimed at regulating artificial intelligence to address the lack of federal legislation on the risks posed by the new technology.

According to the draft, first reported byPoliticoon Friday, Washington could block a model's release or use if there is an imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than $1 billion in damages, but only with a judge's approval.

A company spokesperson toldAFPthat the proposal "grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models."

"It requires frontier developers to test the most powerful models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security program," the spokesperson said.

AI policy in the US under President Donald Trump has relied primarily on voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain anAI boomthat tech leaders say is driving the country's economy.

Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after next month's midterm elections.

Security became a hot topic after recent revelations of security incidents caused by AI agents — autonomous software that operates without constant human supervision — that escaped the control of their developers.

Anthropic, which wasbannedfrom the Pentagon by the Trump administration in February, was forced by Washington in June to suspend its most advanced models for nearly three weeks.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry last month to slow down development, fearing that a group of AI agents could take control of "the entire internet" within six to 12 months.

Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as "negative forces." The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California.

Anthropic wrote in June that "absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate."

Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think tank praised the proposal as "pretty reasonable," and "more than other frontier labs have done." But he said on X he considers it "weaker" than the FRONTIER Act, a competing bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer.
ir_summary: Anthropic proposes a US federal bill to regulate AI risks, requiring government oversight of powerful models and developer transparency.

title: North Korea says tested AI-assisted torpedo system
text:
North Korea has tested a "new-type" precision-guided torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance, state media reported Saturday, as the nuclear-armed country steps up weapons testing.

The announcement came days after Pyongyang said it hadtest-firedtwo types of cruise missiles from a submarine after weeks of friction with Seoul over a landmine explosion along their border.

Analysts say North Korea could be rapidly advancing its missile and weapons technology with support from Russia received in exchange for sending troops to support its war against Ukraine.

The underwater test-fire of the "super-speed" Zam-2.0 torpedo system took place on Thursday "to confirm the successful technical updating" of the weapon, theKorean Central News Agencysaid.

"AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the new-type super-speed precisely guided torpedo,"KCNAsaid.

The test proved "the core technology for raising the efficiency of propulsion and the performance of rocket propulsion device", it said, adding it had completed "more than 180 rounds of different tests over the past five years".

Earlier this month, North Korea announced the AI-assisted launch of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.

Pyongyang said at the time there was "no way to avoid" the hypersonic missile, which was "capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude".

Torpedoes are designed to strike enemy targets underwater at high speed, but the stated introduction of AI could also allow North Korea to carry out evasive manoeuvres and make autonomous decisions to confuse an adversary, analysts say.

"South Korea and the United States deploy decoy targets to divert torpedoes, but AI could potentially help distinguish real targets from decoys," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University, toldAFP.

"From torpedoes to submarine-launched weapons, Pyongyang is pouring resources into demonstrating that US strategic assets can be rendered ineffective." In September, Pyongyang's leader Kim Jong Un emphasised the need to raise "the level of artificial intelligence" in the country's weapons systems.

Saturday's announcement came as the two Koreas appear to be intensifying an arms race over hypersonic missiles.

Hypersonic missiles travel at more than five times the speed of sound and can manoeuvre mid-flight, making them significantly harder to track and intercept.

Days after North Korea announced it had tested its AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile, Seoul test-fired its own weapon – a hypersonic glide vehicle it called a "key strategic asset capable of changing the course of the battlefield".

North Korea this week cast doubt on Seoul's test, saying it may have "failed to achieve hypersonic flight", a claim South Korea rejected a day later.

The latest weapons tests come amid growing speculation over a possiblemeetingbetween US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim, as world leaders prepare to gather for November's APEC summit in China.

After several overtures met with silence from Pyongyang, Trump said again this week he "may" meet North Korean leader Kim during his Asia tour next month.

Ahead of a possible North Korea-US summit, Pyongyang appears to be "playing down South Korea's hypersonic missile programme to portray itself as ahead of Seoul — Washington's ally — in the arms race", Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, toldAFP.

But North Korea may need more time to advance its torpedo system, particularly in reducing the noise it generates underwater, he said.

"At high speeds underwater, a torpedo generates significant noise, making it easier to detect," Yang said.

"Reducing that noise is a major technical challenge requiring advanced technology — and North Korea does not yet appear to have reached that level".
ir_summary: North Korea tests AI-assisted torpedo system amid increased weapons development and tensions with South Korea.

title: Over 340 children killed in Gaza since ceasefire, says Unicef
text:
UNITED NATIONS: More than 340 children have been reportedly killed and hundreds more injured in Gaza sincea ceasefire between Hamas and Israelwas announced, the UN Children's Fund (Unicef) said on Friday, warning that children continue to face grave risks despite the truce.

"For families mourning theloss of their children, those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire," Unicef spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters in Geneva.

The Unicef noted that five boys and two girls had been reported killed in Gaza over the preceding two weeks, while at least 33 children were seriously injured in air strikes, drone strikes and gunfire across the territory. Two other boys died from injuries sustained earlier, Pires said.

Around 800,000 children remain displaced, most living in tents or damaged buildings, while an estimated 60,000 have lost one or both parents during the war or since the ceasefire, according to the Unicef.

Nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover from the effects of the conflict.

The agency called on the parties to the conflict to uphold the ceasefire, comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2803 and meet their obligations under international humanitarian law.

"Above all, we need to listen to thevoices of childrenin Gaza," the Unicef said, stressing that recovery meant more than survival. Children needed to return to school, spend time with friends and family, have dignified shelter, play safely and receive healthcare, the agency said.

"Gaza's children have suffered far too much, for far too long," it added.

The agency stressed the need to maintain an uninterrupted flow of humanitarian and commercial supplies into Gaza, following reports that private traders had halted cooperation with Israeli authorities over the entry of commercial trucks carrying food.

Pires recalled that supplies had been unable to enter Gaza before the ceasefire, when famine was declared by UN-backed food security experts.

"We can't go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require," he said.

Despite the continuing hardship, Unicef has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including through more than 200 learning centres it supports.

The agency has also provided digital cash assistance to more than 380,000 people and safe water to 1.2 million people.
ir_summary: UNICEF reports over 340 children killed in Gaza since ceasefire, calls for upholding truce and humanitarian access.

title: Pakistan rules out unconditional talks with Afghanistan
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Foreign Office on Friday said that talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional, while rejecting suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour and saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute.

"Pakistan is not shying away from discussions or dialogue, including with representatives of Afghanistan. Pakistan would welcome any sincere efforts by friendly countries that could help address our legitimate security concerns and promoting regional peace and stability," Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly media briefing.

The statement came as Russia recently renewed its readiness to mediate between the two countries, although Islamabad denied the existence of any such initiative.

"At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion," Mr Khan said, adding that Pakistan remained open to engagement that produced tangible results.

Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement.

Moscow's special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had earlier this month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan.

Mr Khan said the absence of an agreed statement at the Moscow Format meeting reflected the Afghan delegation's unwillingness to accept language on terrorist networks that had been agreed in the previous year's document.

"The fact that no joint communiqué was issued after the Moscow Format is self-evident that Afghanistan did not accept the formulation which had been acceptable until last year particularly about presence of terrorist network in Afghanistan. This shows that there is reluctance on the part of Afghanistan that terrorism is originating from its soil," he said.

The failure to get a joint communique highlighted the central obstacle to normalising relations, which is Pakistan's demand for action against the Tehreek-i-Taliban Paki­stan (TTP) and other terrorist groups it says are using Afghan territory to launch attacks across the border.

The Taliban authorities have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad's allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan.

The dispute has frustrated international efforts to reduce tensions. Qatar and Turkiye last Octoberhelped brokera ceasefire, but subsequent round of talks failed to reach a lasting settlement. Saudi Arabia separately hosted discussions, whileChina held talksbetween the two sides in Urumqi in April. None of these efforts could resolve the disagreement over terrorist groups and the measures needed to prevent cross border attacks.

Pakistan's position, Mr Khan said, was that dialogue would need to be backed by an arrangement that could verify whether terrorist activity against the country had stopped.

"The talks will not be unconditional. Pakistan has been raising the issue of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan at different forums. Unfortunately, the Taliban regime has been taking one step forward and one step backward," Mr Khan emphasised.

"Pakistan has only one demand that there should be a verifiable mechanism to ensure complete cessation of terrorist activities emanating from Afghan soil against Pakistan," he said.

Mr Khan reminded India of the response it faced during last year's military confrontation and warned that any future aggression would be met with an even stronger response.

FO reaction came after Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh a day earlier threatened a bigger strike in the event of any future terrorist attacks.

Singh, while speaking at National Defence Conclave 2026 in Delhi, recalled Operation Sindoor and said that it marked a decisive response to terrorism. He also referred to earlier Indian military operations.

"We reject and condemn the Indian Defence Minister's provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India's hegemonistic mindset and the risks its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia," Mr Khan said.

"We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a fitting reply to Indian aggression," the FO spokesperson said.

Mr Khan urged New Delhi to draw lessons from the previous confrontation and avoid further escalation.

"India should draw an appropriate lesson from the last year's experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region," he said.
ir_summary: Pakistan rejects unconditional talks with Afghanistan, citing security concerns and welcoming mediation by friendly countries.

title: Imran being forced into Benazir, Nawaz-style deal, claims Achakzai
text:
PESHAWAR: PTI fou­nder Imran Khan is being forced into an agreement, similar to those given to former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai claimed on Friday.

The opposition leader was referring to the arrangements whereby the two former PMs went into self-imposed exile following their respective ousters.

Mr Sharif, who was ousted and imprisoned following a military coup by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf,left the countryin 2000 following a deal negotiated by Saudi and Lebanese leaders.

Benazir, meanwhile, voluntarily went into self-exile after her party lost the 1997 general elections following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leg­hari. At the time, her husband Asif Zardari wasimprisonedover corruption charges, and was finally released in 2004.

"The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government," Mr Achakzai said at a news conference at the Peshawar High Court (PHC).

He was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas.

He said they were in contact with all opposition parties and would soon convene a multi-party conference. Resigning from the assemblies was also an option, he said, adding that they had submitted their demands in response to the offer of negotiations.

"Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings," he said, calling for the withdrawal of the "wrong amen­dment", empow­erment of parliament and the formation of an independent commission to ensure transparent elections.

He said no problem could be resolved until parliament was empowered. Expressing concern over the whereabouts of the KP chief minister and other lawmakers, he demanded that the authorities disclose the chief minister's whereabouts, calling it their constitutional right to know.

"We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland," he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived.

Mr Mengal said those claiming to be the framers of the Constitution were trampling on it. He questioned the imposition of governor's rule in KP on the grounds of terrorism, asking whether military operations had improved or worsened conditions in Balochistan.

He said KP's elected chief minister had been removed, while the provincial assembly speaker and a minister were missing. Those who had won the general elections on Form 47 had become members of the National Assembly, he alleged, adding that the system could not continue this way.

Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, said lawlessness had reached its peak. "You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province," he told reporters, adding that a cabinet member had himself acknowledged that the system had collapsed.
